summary: IGNIS is an interactive research and decision-support prototype that helps engineers and researchers explore fire safety evidence from NASA’s Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) combustion investigations. Rather than presenting papers as an isolated list, IGNIS connects investigation discovery, experimental conditions, source-linked findings, comparisons, habitat scenarios, and exploratory predictive tools. Users can ask which experiments are relevant to a spacecraft or pressurized habitat, inspect what was actually tested, and identify where the available evidence does not support a confident conclusion. Its goal is to make complex microgravity combustion research more accessible, comparable, and actionable while clearly separating verified source provenance from scientific validation
details:
The Problem

Fire behaves differently in microgravity because buoyancy-driven convection is reduced. NASA has investigated ignition, flame spread, smoke and aerosols, and extinction under varied fuels, materials, oxygen concentrations, airflow conditions, and experimental hardware. Those results are valuable for spacecraft, space stations, lunar bases, and pressurized rovers, but can be difficult to locate, compare, and interpret consistently. IGNIS addresses this evidence-to-decision gap.

Our Solution and User Journey

  1. Frame a safety question for a habitable environment, such as material flammability under a proposed oxygen and pressure scenario.
  2. Find relevant PSI investigations through semantic search and explore structured investigation profiles.
  3. Compare studies and test conditions, including oxygen, pressure, airflow, materials, and available measurements. Missing values are explicitly distinguished from out-of-range values.
  4. Inspect source-linked findings, experimental records, and candidate relationships between investigations; identify assumptions, incompatibilities, and gaps in the processed corpus.
  5. Use exploratory models only within their documented scope, and leverage the evidence and limitations to inform preliminary design discussions.

Implemented Modules

  • Interactive web experience: IGNIS landing, investigation browsing, search, comparisons, and history.
  • Research data pipeline: PSI inventory, experiment table mapping, document processing, machine-extracted findings, relations, and scenario coverage.
  • Scientific research API: Structured profiles, semantic search, comparisons, citations, and evidence-aware responses.
  • Design and AI laboratory: Tool-using assistant, environment relevance, and exploratory predictive simulators.
  • Data access: Source data inspection and export routes.
  • 3D educational views: Visual interpretation of selected experiments and historical context (for educational visualization, not physical validation).

Technology and Reproducibility

IGNIS uses a browser-based frontend (HTML/CSS/JavaScript, with Three.js for 3D visualizations), a Python web proxy, FastAPI services, DuckDB/Parquet data storage, multilingual semantic retrieval, and rule-based scientific comparability checks. The tool-using assistant is configured with a hosted open-weight language model, while predictive models operate as bounded exploratory tools.

Evidence Quality and Limitations

The processed dataset encompasses 24 PSI investigations, 22 experimental tables, 1,670 public trial records, and 126 candidate findings. These represent corpus and pipeline counts rather than scientifically confirmed conclusions. All 22 table mappings remain in draft status, and automated quote verification establishes source traceability rather than scientific correctness. Text similarity alone cannot establish confirmation or contradiction between studies, and partial-gravity conditions are not recorded per experimental trial, preventing validated predictions for lunar or Martian gravity.

Illustrative Use Case

An engineer exploring a pressurized lunar habitat can search for material flammability evidence, inspect BASS/BASS-II and Saffire investigations, compare available test conditions with a provisional habitat scenario, and distinguish measured overlap from missing conditions. IGNIS helps identify which studies merit expert review and which additional tests or assumptions remain necessary, supporting preliminary engineering without claiming material certification or final design validation.


Key Project Questions

What does your project do, and how does it work? IGNIS turns dispersed NASA microgravity combustion research into a navigable, source-linked evidence workspace. Users formulate a spacecraft or habitat fire-safety question, retrieve relevant PSI investigations, inspect experimental records, compare reported test conditions, and review evidence alongside explicit uncertainties. The prototype connects a web interface with structured scientific data, retrieval services, and a guarded AI research assistant to support preliminary engineering reasoning.

What benefits does it have? IGNIS reduces the effort required to locate and cross-reference relevant investigations, makes experimental context easier to inspect, and helps users recognize when studies cannot be directly compared. Source traceability and visible missing-data flags support more transparent discussions than unreferenced AI answers, while interactive visualizations make specialized research more approachable.

What is the intended impact? The intended impact is to help researchers, mission designers, and fire-safety engineers use existing NASA combustion knowledge more effectively when identifying hazards and framing design trade-offs for crewed spacecraft and future lunar or Martian habitats.

What tools did you use? The system is built with a web frontend using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, Three.js for interactive 3D views, Python/FastAPI backend services, DuckDB and Parquet for structured data storage, multilingual semantic search, and an AI assistant equipped with tool-use capabilities and deterministic source-citation checks.

How is your project creative? IGNIS is designed around an evidence-to-decision journey rather than a static paper catalogue or a generic chatbot. It combines scenario-oriented exploration, investigation comparisons, traceable source citations, interactive experimental data, and immersive educational visualizations in a single interface. Its distinctive design choice is exposing scientific uncertainty and incompatible test conditions rather than hiding them behind a single confidence score.

What factors did your team consider? The design accounts for the absence of buoyancy-driven convection in microgravity, variations in oxygen concentration, pressure, ventilation, materials, and experimental hardware, as well as the limits of transferring laboratory results to operational spacecraft. On the technical side, it addresses incomplete metadata, AI hallucination risk, cross-experiment comparability, and the strict separation between machine-checked citations and human-reviewed scientific validation.

Use of Super Intelligence (SI)

IGNIS combines complementary AI and computational methods rather than treating a language model as a standalone source of scientific truth:

  • Multilingual semantic retrieval identifies candidate relevant investigations.
  • Extraction pipelines isolate claims and quotations from source documents.
  • Deterministic checks verify whether cited passages are traceable to the source text.
  • Structured comparison layers evaluate potential relationships across experimental conditions and concept mappings.
  • Tool-using assistant & predictive models orchestrate specialized retrieval and simulation functions, returning bounded exploratory estimates alongside explicit validation warnings.

The architecture is engineered to expose uncertainty: model-generated findings are clearly distinguished from peer-reviewed conclusions, text similarity is not treated as scientific agreement, and missing measurements are flagged rather than inferred.

NASA Data

IGNIS utilizes data from NASA Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI), focusing on combustion investigations relevant to fire prevention, detection, and suppression. Key investigation families included in the system are:

  • BASS / BASS-II and Saffire: Solid material flammability and flame spread.
  • SAME / SAME-R: Smoke and aerosol characterization.
  • FLEX / FLEX-2: Droplet combustion and extinction.
  • ACME: Gaseous combustion phenomena.

The platform retains investigation identifiers, experimental metadata, and traceable quoted evidence across the ingested subset of the PSI archive.
